package_info.why_malicious: The report does not describe a specific software package or codebase. Instead, it analyzes phishing tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) that use brand impersonation in emails. These include embedding brand logos as base64-encoded images, fetching images from attacker-controlled remote servers, attaching images or PDFs with brand logos, and inserting brand-related keywords in email content. These behaviors are malicious at the campaign level, aiming to deceive recipients and bypass security controls.

execution_context.trigger: When the phishing email is opened by the recipient
execution_context.file_location: HTML body of the phishing email

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the phishing email is opened by the recipient, the HTML code renders a base64-encoded image directly within the email body, displaying a brand logo to the user, which increases the perceived legitimacy of the email and encourages user trust.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Embedding brand logos as base64-encoded images is a common phishing tactic to evade email security filters that block external image loads, making the email appear more authentic and increasing the likelihood of successful deception.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate brand communications typically reference images hosted on official domains or content delivery networks, not base64-encoded images embedded directly in the email body.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some marketing or transactional emails may use base64-encoded images for design or tracking, but this is rare for major brands and usually not for logos.
key_indicators: Presence of base64-encoded image data in email HTML
Brand logos embedded as data URIs instead of being loaded from official domains
Unusually large HTML email size due to embedded image data

execution_context.trigger: When the phishing email is opened by the recipient
execution_context.file_location: HTML body of the phishing email

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the phishing email is opened by the recipient, the HTML code causes the email client to fetch a brand logo image from an attacker-controlled remote server, resulting in the display of the logo in the email and potentially allowing the attacker to track email opens via network requests.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Fetching images from attacker-controlled domains enables both brand impersonation and tracking of email opens, and may also be used to deliver further malicious content.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate brand emails host images on official, trusted domains using HTTPS, not on unknown or suspicious third-party servers, especially not over unencrypted HTTP.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some marketing platforms use third-party image hosting for analytics, but reputable brands rarely use non-brand domains for logos, and almost never use HTTP.
key_indicators: Image URLs in email HTML pointing to domains not associated with the impersonated brand
Use of HTTP (not HTTPS) for image delivery
Remote image loads from recently registered or low-reputation domains

execution_context.trigger: When the phishing email is opened and the recipient views or opens the attachment
required_permissions: none (email client renders or previews attachment)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the phishing email is opened and the recipient views or opens the attachment, the attached image or PDF file displays a brand logo, reinforcing the impersonation and increasing the likelihood that the recipient will trust the email and follow embedded instructions or links.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Including brand logos as standalone attachments is a tactic to bypass image-blocking protections in email clients and to make phishing emails appear more authentic, especially when the attachment name matches a well-known brand.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate brand communications rarely send logos as separate attachments, especially in unsolicited emails or simple notifications.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some onboarding or marketing emails may include branded PDFs or images, but this is uncommon for simple notifications and typically accompanied by clear context.
key_indicators: Unsolicited image or PDF attachments with filenames matching well-known brands
Attachment names such as logo.pdf, logo.png, or brandname_logo.pdf
Attachments containing only a brand logo with no additional legitimate content

execution_context.trigger: When the phishing email is opened by the recipient
execution_context.file_location: HTML body of the phishing email

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the phishing email is opened by the recipient, the HTML code inserts brand-related keywords (such as 'Microsoft SharePoint') into the email body, presenting the appearance of a trusted service and increasing the likelihood that the recipient will engage with the email.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Inserting brand-related keywords in the email body is a social engineering tactic designed to deceive recipients by leveraging the trust associated with well-known brands.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate emails from brands use official templates and consistent branding, not arbitrary or contextually inappropriate text insertions.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some newsletters or notifications may mention brand names, but not in a deceptive or misleading context.
key_indicators: Brand names or service keywords used out of context in email content
Presence of brand-related keywords in emails from non-brand domains or suspicious senders
Inconsistent branding or formatting compared to legitimate communications

attack_chain.action: Phishing email is crafted with embedded or attached brand logos and brand-related keywords to impersonate a trusted company.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim opens the email, perceives it as legitimate, and is more likely to interact with its content.

attack_chain.action: Victim is lured into clicking a malicious link, calling a phone number, or opening an attachment, potentially leading to credential theft, malware delivery, or further compromise.
attack_chain.leads_to: Exfiltration of sensitive information or further compromise of the victim's system or account.

behavioral_signatures: Emails containing base64-encoded images displaying brand logos in the HTML body
Emails fetching images from domains not associated with the impersonated brand, especially over HTTP
Emails with image or PDF attachments named after well-known brands (e.g., logo.pdf, brandname_logo.png)
Emails containing brand-related keywords or service names in unusual or out-of-context locations within the email body
file_indicators: Attachments with filenames such as logo.pdf, logo.png, or brandname_logo.pdf
HTML emails containing tags with base64-encoded image data (data:image/*;base64,...)
Emails with attachments that contain only a brand logo image or PDF
network_indicators: Image fetch requests to domains not matching the official domains of the impersonated brand
HTTP (not HTTPS) image requests initiated by email clients when rendering email content
Network requests to recently registered or low-reputation domains from email content
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor inbound emails for HTML content containing base64-encoded images, tags referencing non-brand or suspicious domains, and attachments with filenames matching well-known brands. Flag emails that use brand names or service keywords in unusual contexts or from untrusted senders. Correlate these indicators with known phishing IOCs, block or quarantine suspicious messages, and alert security teams for further investigation.
